samples.text:
Nowadays, artificial intelligence (AI) is used more and more in offices, factories and shops. Many people are worried that they will lose their job because computers can do their work faster and cheaper. This essay will discuss the problems this might cause and how governments and individuals can prepare.

The main problem is unemployment. If companies use AI to do tasks like answering customers, writing reports or checking documents, they will need less workers. Many people, especially who do simple and repetitive jobs, can lose their income. This can lead to poverty and stress for families. Another problem is that the gap between rich and poor may become bigger. The owners of technology companies will earn a lot of money, but normal workers will earn less or nothing. As a result, some people may feel angry and there can be problems in the society.

To prepare for these changes, governments have an important role. Firstly, they should give free training courses for adults, so workers can learn new skills, for example using technology or working in health care, where humans are still needed. Secondly, governments should support people who lose their jobs by giving them money for a period while they are looking for another job.

Individuals also need to prepare. They should keep learning during all their life and not think that their education finish at university. For example, an accountant can learn how to use AI tools, so he can work together with the technology instead to be replaced by it.

In conclusion, AI may cause unemployment and more inequality. However, if governments provide training and support, and individuals continue learning, people can adapt to these changes.
samples.why: Covers problems and both government and individual preparation · individual section underdeveloped · clear paragraphing with basic linking · adequate vocabulary · several errors in quantifiers, relative clauses and verb patterns.

samples.text:
The rapid spread of artificial intelligence in the workplace has raised widespread concern that many jobs will soon be carried out by machines. This development could create serious problems, and both governments and individuals need to prepare for it.

The most obvious risk is job losses, particularly in roles that involve routine tasks. Customer service, data entry, basic accounting and some types of administrative work can already be partly automated, and workers in these areas may find that their skills are no longer in demand. For those affected, losing a job can mean not only financial hardship but also a loss of confidence and identity. On a wider scale, AI could increase inequality. The benefits of automation are likely to go mainly to companies and highly skilled workers, while people in lower-paid jobs face greater insecurity, which may lead to social tension.

Governments have a key role in managing this transition. They should invest in affordable retraining programmes that allow adults to move into growing sectors, such as healthcare, green energy or technology-related work. Education systems also needs to adapt, placing more emphasis on skills that machines find difficult to replicate, such as critical thinking, creativity and interpersonal communication. In addition, stronger social safety nets, including unemployment support linked to training, would help people through periods between jobs.

Individuals, meanwhile, cannot rely entirely on the state. The most important step is to adopt a habit of lifelong learning and to stay informed about how technology is affecting their industry. Rather than seeing AI purely as a threat, workers who learn to use these tools effectively are likely to become more valuable to employers, not less.

In conclusion, AI may cause unemployment and widen inequality, but with retraining, educational reform and a willingness to keep learning, societies can adapt to these changes successfully.
samples.why: Clear position · problems extended at personal and social level · separate, focused paragraphs for governments and individuals · good collocation (social safety nets, lifelong learning) · one agreement slip.

samples.text:
As artificial intelligence moves from research laboratories into everyday workplaces, anxiety about the future of employment has grown. Although new technologies have historically created new kinds of work as well as destroying old ones, the speed and breadth of AI adoption could make this transition unusually disruptive, and preparing for it is a shared responsibility of governments and individuals.

The most immediate concern is displacement. AI systems can already draft documents, analyse data and handle customer queries, which places many clerical, administrative and even some professional roles at risk. Workers whose skills become redundant in mid-career may struggle to find comparable employment, facing not only a loss of income but a loss of status and purpose. There is also a distributional problem. The gains from automation are likely to flow disproportionately to those who own the technology and to highly skilled specialists, while less qualified workers bear most of the risk, potentially widening inequality and fuelling political discontent.

Governments should focus on easing the transition rather than resisting technological change. Large-scale, accessible retraining, ideally designed with employers so that it leads to real vacancies, would help displaced workers move into expanding fields. Schools and universities need to prioritise capabilities that complement AI, such as judgement, creativity and collaboration, alongside the digital literacy needed to work with intelligent systems. A modernised safety net, linking income support to training, would give people the security to retrain rather than accept the first available job.

Individuals, for their part, can reduce their vulnerability by treating learning as a career-long process. Becoming proficient with the AI tools relevant to their field, and cultivating distinctly human strengths such as persuasion and empathy, makes workers more likely to be augmented by technology than replaced by it.

In conclusion, AI threatens displacement and greater inequality, but coordinated investment in skills and social protection, combined with personal adaptability, can make the transition far more manageable.
samples.why: All parts of the question fully addressed, with distinct roles for governments and individuals · well-developed, qualified arguments · skilful paragraphing · precise vocabulary (displacement, distributional, augmented) · wide range of error-free structures.
